**Moral psychology** — morality as a natural phenomenon — moral judgement, emotion and norms, and their evolution, development and variation across cultures; descriptive, where ethics is normative (group: philosophy; ADR-018).

| [THEORY-121](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-121.md) v5 | Moral responsibility requires guidance control, moderate reasons-responsiveness of the agent's own actual-sequence mechanism, and not regulative control over alternative possibilities, so responsibility is compatible with causal determinism | Fischer and Ravizza, in their own précis ([LIT-728](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-728.md), read): moral responsibility requires guidance control, not regulative control over alternatives. Guidance control is acting from a mechanism one has made one's own by taking responsibility for it, which is moderately reasons-responsive: regularly receptive to reasons, some moral, and at least weakly reactive. Fischer's 1987 paper ([LIT-687](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-687.md), read) is the weak-responsiveness origin. The view is compatible with causal determinism. | Active |
| [THEORY-122](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-122.md) | Moral responsibility requires the normative competence to recognise and act on the True and the Good, which identification with one's own motives does not supply | Susan Wolf's Reason View, reported second-hand: the primary texts are unread. McKenna and Coates ([LIT-291](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-291.md), §4.3) report that for Wolf free will is the ability to act in accord with the True and the Good, an anchor outside the agent's psychology. Talbert ([LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md), §§3.1.1, 3.2) reports her case against deep-self or Real Self views and the JoJo case: JoJo identifies wholly with the cruel values his father raised him in, yet is not responsible, because he cannot appreciate that they are wrong. The claim is a necessary condition. It does not by itself say whether the ability must include being able to do otherwise; that is [THEORY-118](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-118.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-147](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-147.md) | Deep responsibility is not limited to the moral, and attributability and accountability are independent kinds of it rather than two levels: accountability needs only that the agent acted as she ought not to, was in a position to know it, and that acting so was up to her, while what makes a self a fit target of the reactive attitudes is plausibly that it can perceive, understand and appreciate the world as we do | Wolf (2015), [LIT-747](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-747.md), the 2013 Routledge Lecture. We are deeply, not merely causally, responsible for nonmoral traits and art, by the self-disclosure view. Watson's two-level view, accountability as attributability plus control, is rejected: a stipulated psychopath may be accountable for acts whose source is not attributable to him. Fitness for reactive attitudes is, on Wolf's hunch, being an intelligent self. Proposed: the positive view is her hunch. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-435](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-435.md) | In Moral Foundations Questionnaire responses, Care and Fairness are endorsed across the political spectrum, while Loyalty, Authority and Sanctity rise toward the conservative end, in every world region sampled | Graham, Haidt et al. (2013), [LIT-499](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-499.md), read in [NOTE-396](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-396.md), reporting large internet samples in twelve world regions; and Atari et al. (2023), [LIT-500](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-500.md) ([NOTE-398](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-398.md)), with the MFQ-2 in 19 nations. The profile is robust as a description of self-report. It is a finding about what people say they weigh, mostly online, mostly English-speaking, and mostly WEIRD; and Purity, which carries the steepest gradient, fails cross-national invariance in the MFQ-2. | Active |
| [THEORY-457](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-457.md) | When people can choose their cooperation partners and have equal outside options, the stable division of jointly produced gains is in proportion to each partner's contribution, and partner choice selects for a genuine sense of fairness as proportionality | Baumard, André & Sperber (2013), [LIT-508](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-508.md), read in [NOTE-407](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-407.md), with its 28 commentaries and Response. The pairwise result is cited from another paper; the extension to effort and talent is unproven by the authors' own statement. The evidence is a reinterpretation of dictator, ultimatum, trust and public-goods results as allocation by entitlement. The authors disagree among themselves about whether purity, loyalty and kin care are moral at all. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-468](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-468.md) | Morality is the set of solutions to recurrent problems of cooperation, so each of the seven cooperation problems game theory identifies yields a moral domain valued in every culture, and behaviour unrelated to cooperation is morally neutral | Curry (2016), [LIT-503](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-503.md), read in [NOTE-408](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-408.md), with its two tests, [LIT-047](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-047.md) ([NOTE-034](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-034.md)) and [LIT-496](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-496.md) ([NOTE-412](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-412.md)). The positive half has support: the seven are described as good wherever ethnographers record them, and questionnaire items for them form seven factors. The negative half, that nothing else is moralized, is the theory's own stated prediction (p. 40). No study in the programme has tested it blind, and where non-cooperative items appear, the programme's own data show them moralized. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-494](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-494.md) | Puritanical norms against harmless bodily pleasures are cooperative morality: people believe cooperation needs self-control, which indulgence erodes and discipline trains, and condemn indulgence as an indirect threat to cooperation | Fitouchi, André & Baumard (2021), [LIT-101](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-101.md), read in [NOTE-132](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-132.md). In the authors' vignette studies (N > 1,100), perceived loss of self-control mediated all of the perceived effect of indulgence on cooperativeness. The rest is a review: disgust does not amplify condemnation once harm is controlled, and a society's valuing of self-control predicts its hygiene norms better than pathogen threat. The account is agnostic about whether the norms work, excludes contamination purity by definition, and has shown that people hold the belief, not that the belief made the norms. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-495](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-495.md) | The human sense of obligation is internalized pressure from a joint agent 'we' to do what 'we' expect of me; it appears around age three inside joint commitments, where children, unlike chimpanzees, protest, repair, take leave and share equally with a committed partner as they do not with others | Tomasello (2019), [LIT-125](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-125.md), read in [NOTE-185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-185.md). A synthesis of developmental and comparative experiments, mostly from the author's lab, on WEIRD children and chimpanzees; no new data. The behavioural contrasts between committed and side-by-side play are moderately supported. That they reflect felt obligation, rather than prosociality or learned scripts, is argued, not shown. It explains the sense of obligation, not what anyone is obliged to do, as the author concedes. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-505](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-505.md) | Questionnaire items written for morality-as-cooperation's seven domains form seven factors when rated for relevance to moral decisions, in the UK, the US and Turkey, but not when rated as agreement with moral statements, and the two formats cannot be pooled into seven domains | Curry, Jones Chesters & Van Lissa (2019), [LIT-496](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-496.md), read in [NOTE-412](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-412.md), and the independent Turkish validation by Yilmaz, Harma & Doğruyol (2021), [LIT-513](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-513.md) ([NOTE-397](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-397.md)). Relevance items fit seven factors in all three samples (CFI .98 UK, .95 Turkey). Judgement items do not (CFI .87, .83), and a seven-domain model of both fails (CFI .73, .75). The items were written from the theory and selected for fit within each domain, several subscales correlate above .8, and no item is non-cooperative. This is evidence about the instrument's structure, not about what morality contains. | Active |
| [THEORY-539](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-539.md) | Moral judgment draws on several innately prepared intuitive foundations, at least Care, Fairness, Loyalty, Authority and Sanctity, each a response to a different adaptive challenge, and Sanctity descends from pathogen avoidance rather than from cooperation | Graham, Haidt et al. (2013), [LIT-499](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-499.md), read in [NOTE-396](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-396.md); its first statement, Haidt & Joseph (2004), [LIT-502](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-502.md) ([NOTE-400](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-400.md)); and the MFQ-2, Atari et al. (2023), [LIT-500](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-500.md) ([NOTE-398](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-398.md)). Pluralism has moderate support. The particular list does not: its evidence table gives Sanctity no primate or infant evidence and Authority no infant evidence, the foundations were matched to existing evolutionary models rather than derived, and the disgust findings behind Sanctity were later disputed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-558](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-558.md) | Moral judgment is usually caused by quick affective intuitions, and moral reasoning is usually a post-hoc search for supporting reasons that changes judgments mainly by triggering intuitions in other people | Haidt (2001), [LIT-511](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-511.md), read in [NOTE-403](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-403.md): the social intuitionist model. Its case rests mostly on non-moral evidence about automaticity, motivated reasoning and confabulation, carried over by argument. Its direct moral evidence is that harmless taboo violations are condemned and that affect predicts the condemnation better than perceived harm. The author calls it "a plausible alternative", not "an established fact". The disgust manipulations that were its direct causal evidence were later disputed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-613](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-613.md) | The Moral Foundations Questionnaire-2's six factors, Care, Equality, Proportionality, Loyalty, Authority and Purity, fit across 19 nations, Equality and Proportionality are nearly uncorrelated in WEIRD nations, and the US split between individualizing and binding foundations appears in only three national networks | Atari, Haidt, Graham, Koleva, Stevens & Dehghani (2023), [LIT-500](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-500.md), read in [NOTE-398](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-398.md). 36 items, developed in 25 populations, fit six factors in 19 nations (ESEM CFI .979). Equality and Proportionality correlate .21 on average, from .47 to −.04. Purity alone fails intercept invariance, and it carries the headline that Purity is the least WEIRD foundation. The samples are online and about 200 per nation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-626](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-626.md) | Moral judgments are made relative to the social relationship an act is taken to occur within: each of four relational models (communal sharing, authority ranking, equality matching, market pricing) carries a moral motive (Unity, Hierarchy, Equality, Proportionality), so the same act can be required under one and wrong under another | Rai & Fiske (2011), [LIT-507](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-507.md), read in [NOTE-405](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-405.md). A theoretical review with no new data. Its strongest support is cited work on relational framing and on morally motivated violence. Which model is in force is read off after the fact, so the central claim risks being unfalsifiable as stated. Purity and ingroup loyalty are assigned to one motive, Unity, by argument. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-632](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-632.md) | Purity is moralized in self-report: in morality-as-cooperation's own questionnaire studies, purity items are rated about as morally relevant as loyalty and authority items, and harmless purity violations are condemned, so that theory's prediction that non-cooperative behaviour is morally neutral fails unless purity is itself cooperative | Curry, Jones Chesters & Van Lissa (2019), [LIT-496](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-496.md), read in [NOTE-412](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-412.md), against the prediction stated in Curry (2016), [LIT-503](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-503.md) ([NOTE-408](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-408.md)), with the harmless-wrongs studies Haidt (2001) reports, [LIT-511](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-511.md) ([NOTE-403](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-403.md)). In two samples, MFQ purity items are rated morally relevant at the level of ingroup and authority items, and the authors concede this "appear[s] to contradict" the theory. | [THEORY-653](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-653.md) | In the ethnographic record of the 60-society HRAF Probability Sample, seven cooperative behaviours are described as good in 961 of 962 valenced mentions, but each is recorded in between 90% and 15% of the societies, and the coding could barely have registered a negative | Curry, Mullins & Whitehouse (2019), [LIT-047](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-047.md), read in [NOTE-034](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-034.md). Coding eHRAF paragraphs on the 60 Probability Sample societies found 962 morally valenced mentions of helping kin, helping one's group, reciprocating, bravery, deference, dividing disputed resources and respecting possession; 961 were positive. Presence ran from property (54/60) to fairness (9/60) and tracked ethnographic coverage (r = .43). The behaviours are defined in virtue terms and conflicts were set aside, so a negative was nearly impossible to code. It is a description of the coded record, not a test of whether morality is only about cooperation. | Active |
| [THEORY-663](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-663.md) | Altruism between non-relatives can be selected when each act costs the giver less than it benefits the recipient, the same partners meet often and symmetrically, and help is withheld from those who do not return it; in humans, moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy and guilt are adaptations that regulate such exchange, and selection then favours sham versions of each and the ability to detect them | Trivers (1971), [LIT-510](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-510.md), read in full in [NOTE-402](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-402.md). A verbal model, with a Prisoner's Dilemma sketch Hamilton communicated, followed by a functional account of the human emotions that would regulate reciprocity. The model is plausible and was later formalized. The psychology is fitted to 1960s social-psychology findings, mostly on American students, and the heritability of the dispositions is assumed. Trivers knows "of no psychological studies on the detection of sham moralistic aggression and sham guilt" (p. 51). His "unfairness" is inequity in exchange, not the division of a disputed resource. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-892](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-892.md) v2 | Psychopathy as the PCL-R measures it is one dimensional construct rather than a type: its items form four correlated factors, interpersonal, affective, lifestyle and antisocial, explained by one superordinate factor, and its affective features are tied psychometrically, genetically and longitudinally to its antisocial ones, so that no one component is its essence | Hare and Neumann (2008), read in [NOTE-1094](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1094.md). The PCL-R's twenty items load on four correlated factors, which pair into Factor 1 (interpersonal, affective) and Factor 2 (lifestyle, antisocial) and are explained by one superordinate factor. The affective features are tied to the antisocial ones, so the authors deny that any component is the disorder's core, and they read the evidence as dimensional. Filed for the record's question on corporate psychopathy, which asks which of these features could be said of a corporation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1352](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1352.md) v2 | In Van Lange and Bergmann's model, human cooperation is readily sustained between individuals, above all in dyads, through precise reciprocity, empathy and a partner who cannot be excluded at no cost, and is fragile between groups: categorization alone yields mistrust and in-group favouritism by bounded reciprocity, observed out-group favouritism hardens it into distrust, and chiefly negative interdependence, real or perceived, turns that into costly competition, aggression and hate, so that the processes that build in-group cooperation can fuel intergroup conflict | Van Lange and Bergmann (2026), [LIT-2002](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2002.md), read in [NOTE-1537](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1537.md). The refinement that matters to the record: lower cooperation between groups does not need conflicting interests, and harm to the out-group does. | Active |
| [THEORY-1529](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1529.md) | Human cooperation is readily sustained between individuals, above all in dyads, through precise reciprocity, empathy and a partner who cannot be excluded at no cost, and is fragile between groups: categorization alone yields mistrust and in-group favouritism by bounded reciprocity, observed out-group favouritism hardens it into distrust, and chiefly negative interdependence, real or perceived, turns that into costly competition, aggression and hate, so that the processes that build in-group cooperation can fuel intergroup conflict | The thesis Van Lange and Bergmann (2026), [LIT-2002](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2002.md), propose, filed beside the Active report [THEORY-1352](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1352.md) by the twenty-seventh status review ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md), [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1).
